newsitem.title: INDIA: Red tape ruins tax breaks in India infrastructure.
newsitem.headline: Red tape ruins tax breaks in India infrastructure.

text.p: Tax concessions make India's infrastructure policy attractive, but political confusion and bureaucratic bungling are putting off foreign investors, analysts said on Thursday.
"The fiscal part is a complete non-issue. Tax breaks as they stand are attractive enough," columnist Swaminathan S. Anklesaria Aiyar told Reuters. "The problems are entirely procedural."

Analysts said politicians of the ruling United Front coalition were shifting from commitments on specific issues, harming tax incentives designed to lure billions of dollars to build roads, airports, power plants, ports and telecommunications.
Political confusion, litigation challenging projects, land acquisition problems and several levels of technical approvals for power firms irked investors, Aiyar said.

India, which ended state monopolies in infrastructure under a liberalisation programme launched in 1991, needs $79 billion to ease power shortages, and $12 billion to double telephone penetration to a modest target of two per hundred people.

India offers a five-year tax holiday for infrastructure firms, and exempts 30 percent of profits for the next five years. In power and telecommunications, equipment imports are permitted at a concessional 20 percent duty.
New Delhi has also allowed capital gains tax exemption on infrastructure securities issued by mutual funds and some income tax reliefs for individuals investing in infrastructure.

"All this (exemptions) can be useful only if you begin financial closures (for projects)," said Gopal Rajagopalan, executive director at Infrastructure Leasing and Financial Services (IL&FS), a leading infrastructure finance company.
"There is a lot of activity but no action. However, we are hopeful that a number of projects will reach financial closure and provide a leitmotif for the future," he said.
Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram will present the budget for 1997/98 (April-March) on February 28.
One industry expert, who did not want to be named, said there was a case for tax exemptions at the state government level, but added that easier approvals were more important.
Industry officials say there is also a case for expanding the official definition of investments to help infrastructure finance companies, which sometimes invest in other areas.
But the key issue was clarity on policies, analysts said.

Aiyar cited the example of an approved plan to let Singaporean investors build, own and operate a $335-million airport in Bangalore, which Civil Aviation Minister Chand Mahal Ibrahim now insists must be transferred to the government.

Similarly, investors who committed huge investments to set up mobile phone networks were hurt this month by a sudden government decision to hike charges on calls made from fixed telephones, which upset their calculations, he said.
Analysts said India's bid to develop a robust long-term debt market to help fund a voracious hunger for infrastructure also faced temporary problems linked to macroeconomic policies.
New Delhi has failed to lure foreign lenders despite high interest rates because of perceived risks in exchange rates and a lack of liqudity in the Indian bond market, they said.
"People don't have full faith in India yet," Aiyar said. "The entire (debt) market needs to be developed."

India has launched reforms to create a robust secondary market in bonds, and also last month formed the Infrastructure Development Finance Company (IDFC), which is expected to guarantee payments to fund infrastructure.
Rajagopalan said underwriting and guarantees by IDFC will help create a better framework for infrastructure investors.
But judicial reforms to end a spate of court cases challenging projects was more important, Aiyar said.
